item.title: The Rules Cannot Change Only for Young Mathematicians: AI and the future of a mathematical career
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts

item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Postdoc

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

I am a postdoctoral mathematician working in partial differential equations, and I love what I do. I have preferred doing mathematics to expressing opinions in public, but the rapid changes of recent months have made that difficult.

I am writing neither to defend a complete ban on AI nor to celebrate its unrestricted use, but because I no longer know what rules I am expected to follow, what work will count as my own, or how today’s decisions will affect my career.

For an established professor, uncertainty about the future may be a subject for an interesting essay; for a doctoral student or postdoc, it can determine whether years of work lead to a job. The same advice does not carry the same risk for everyone.

My concern is not only what AI can do to mathematics, but what mathematicians and institutions are choosing to do to one another during this transition.

1. We are told that priority will matter less, but the race suggests otherwise

A recurring message in the recent debate is that recognition should move from being first toward understanding proofs, explaining their ideas, and making them useful to others.

In Mathematics in the age of AI, Terence Tao argues for less emphasis on proof generation and being first. Amit Harlev goes further: “when a result is proven by an AI, priority should carry no reward.” Timothy Gowers predicts that the credit system will collapse, while defending credit as long as careers depend on it. Benoit Henry questions whether a theorem belongs to whoever obtains it first when someone else could quickly do so with a similar system. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Bryna Kra offers a concrete proposal: “Journals need to distinguish and credit the roles of discovery, proof, formalization and explanation.” Grant Sanderson observes that “every AI-generated proof is born an unsolved exposition problem.” [5, 6]

I welcome greater credit for explanation, but cannot behave as though that transition has happened while the consequences of being second remain uncertain. A postdoc cannot pay rent with a prediction that exposition will eventually become prestigious.

The possibility that another person or laboratory could obtain a proof quickly can intensify the pressure to announce first, even as we are asked to slow down, check the literature, understand everything, and write carefully.

Nor do I accept that mathematics was always about understanding rather than solving problems: I value both learning a beautiful argument and finding one that did not previously exist. I do not want either experience dismissed merely because the other may be easier to preserve.

The familiar name “Fermat’s little theorem” reminds me that discovery, proof, and naming are not the same thing. Historical names offer no reliable rulebook for present-day authorship; we need to distinguish priority, authorship, attribution, and understanding explicitly.

2. What exactly does an AI-generated proof entitle its producer to claim?

Jihao Liu states the practical dilemma unusually clearly:

“Consider the following situation. I use AI to produce a paper whose result is important. What should I do?

  1. I post the paper to arXiv. Then I am criticized for not having verified the paper in detail. This goes against my values as a mathematician.
  2. I do not post the paper anywhere. But what if someone else obtains the result and posts it before me? In that case I lose the credit.” [7]

He posts some machine-checked, not yet human-verified papers on a separate webpage rather than arXiv, and requires a timestamp when recognizing prior independent work. [7]

Liu is frank about protecting priority, but the order troubles me: secure the claim first, complete verification and repair attribution afterward. Treating credit as his to grant strikes me as cynical. His offers of shared credit and coauthorship recognize the value of checking, simplifying, and explaining, but leave unclear what the announcement reserves and what later contributors can earn. [7]

What credit has the initial producer earned before these other contributions have been made? Does a public timestamp establish priority for a theorem, a candidate argument, or merely a generated document? If the proof is correct but its attribution incomplete, what is owed to the people whose ideas supplied most of it?

Marco Trombetti’s ProofForum proposal distinguishes generating, checking, repairing, simplifying, and explaining without endorsing Liu’s entire policy: “verification could itself become a visible mathematical contribution.” Recognition need not stop with the generator, and credibility can develop through public examination. [8] That may be useful, but a record of contributions is not yet an agreed system for allocating jobs, prizes, publishing rights, or theorem names.

Ruodu Wang supports human understanding and rewriting, but identifies the incentive problem: “Being the second to solve a problem has low or no value.” His model rewards posting AI output immediately over taking time to understand and rewrite it. [9] Even a reduced but positive reward for first place preserves that disadvantage if second place earns nothing; Wang’s argument is that careful work needs changed incentives, not advice alone. [9]

Removing priority creates another difficulty: junior researchers depend on the problems they solve, rather than the established reputations and other recognized roles of senior mathematicians. Wang writes: “I do not see a good system of evaluating junior mathematicians.” A new ideal is not yet a viable career. [9]

We cannot preserve the reward for speed, demand slow and careful work, and leave the people with the least job security to absorb the conflict.

3. The Navier–Stokes dispute: different results, unresolved standards

The September controversy involving Tristan Buckmaster, Levent Alpöge, and OpenAI left me with a bitter feeling. As a PDE researcher, I wanted to understand both the mathematics and its implications for research practice.

The mathematical claims should first be kept distinct. OpenAI’s September 8 announcement claimed a smooth-forcing Navier–Stokes blow-up result establishing alternatives C and D of the Millennium Prize formulation, alongside a separate unforced Euler result. It distinguishes these from Alpöge and Buckmaster’s forced Euler work and denies that their unpublished work or recent Codex prompts influenced its system. These are OpenAI’s stated claims and account. [10]

In the Q&A of Buckmaster’s September 23rd NYU talk, he says: “Those physical mechanisms that I can explain to you guys came out from LLM.” In his account, AI supplied important mechanisms while human expertise directed the search and helped reconstruct the argument. A label such as “Alpöge–Buckmaster, 2026” therefore needs a clear account of what the researchers proposed, what the systems generated, and who verified and rewrote the proof. [12]

He also describes working with Alpöge through internal models: “it’s not just internal models it’s internal compute.” His point that many agents can matter as much as a better model distinguishes their resources from an ordinary subscription. [12]

Buckmaster questions credit based on “who does something the fastest” and says: “I think this race dynamics doesn’t make sense.” WIRED reports that he released unfinished papers to get ahead of OpenAI’s announcement and accepted responsibility for cleaning them up. Wanting priority to matter less while protecting work under unchanged rules is understandable—and precisely the dilemma younger mathematicians face. The question is not whether one researcher should have solved the incentive problem alone, but whether the community can advise young mathematicians to leave the race while continuing to reward those who enter it. [12, 11]

As of 1 October, more than three weeks after the 7 September announcement, I had not found a revised exposition of the forced Euler proof that resolved my readability concerns. Expecting a world-class fluid dynamics expert such as Buckmaster to produce one does not settle what recognition the initial release deserves. [27]

If an unfinished announcement preserves recognition while a readable proof follows later, is the same option open to a doctoral student or postdoc? What standard of verification and exposition must be met before release, and what recognition remains available to someone who waits?

Buckmaster’s talk and NYU’s announcement explicitly credit Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa’s program and strategy, yet public attention can favor the final announcement over the work that made it possible. [12, 27]

Neither Isabella Ward’s 19 September WIRED article, “Mathematicians Feel Threatened by AI. They Can’t Quit It,” nor the 8 September OfficeChai report, “OpenAI Says It Didn’t See Any Of Buckmaster And Alpöge’s Work While Resolving Navier-Stokes,” names Córdoba or Martínez-Zoroa. My concern is that press coverage of priority disputes in the AI era will tend to focus on who obtained or announced a result first, while overlooking the foundational mathematical work—and the people behind it—that made those AI-assisted discoveries possible. [11, 28]

4. This is not an abstract problem for me

I have checked and rewritten an AI-generated proof of a problem I had not worked on for roughly ten years, but have not published it. A group I will not name is pursuing the same question; as far as I know, they have not resolved it, and my argument appears to take a different route from their earlier attempts. Should I post it with a detailed account of the AI contribution, contact the group first, or offer collaboration? If I present the result at a conference, should I write “Theorem [my name, 2026]” on the slide, and would publishing it help my career, damage my reputation, or both?

I am not asking to claim someone else’s ideas, but what credit checking and rewriting earns; that cannot depend on which influential mathematician is asked.

Meanwhile, I am finishing a substantial article developed over about a year with pen and paper, not with AI. Almost daily, I fear being scooped by someone, perhaps using AI, who posts first: my understanding would remain, but the publication opportunity and recognition for a year of independent work might not.

Antonio Auffinger’s Open problems, open mathematics warns that others can quickly complete a publicly shared strategy, making unfinished ideas risky to share. His call to reshape incentives aims to protect openness for the least secure researchers. [13] I want to continue sharing ideas, asking colleagues questions, and doing careful work without making secrecy, haste, and suspicion the rational way to survive.

5. Recognition, jobs, and the cost of disclosure

Another part of the debate makes these choices even more difficult: some mathematicians do not merely question the value of AI-generated papers, but predict reputational damage for AI users or propose institutional preferences against their work.

In Where I Stand on AI, Vladimir Lazić predicts that attaching one’s name to a partially AI-produced paper can destroy a mathematician’s reputation. Addressing researchers without tenure, he writes:

“you will never get tenure, unless you are being pushed by someone in your camp who has tenure.” [14]

Although this is a prediction rather than evidence about hiring committees generally, a junior researcher cannot ignore the possibility that some evaluators share that attitude.

Donatella Iacono, explicitly following Lazić’s principles, states: “I do not support hiring of academic staff who use AI as a substitute for their own work.” She takes the same position on supervising doctoral and postdoctoral researchers. [32]

Max Weinreich goes beyond predicting reputational consequences: in The crisis of AI-generated mathematics, he proposes “reserving hire lines for mathematicians who eschew AI” and “valuing AI-free papers more highly in tenure promotion.” These are proposals for allocating opportunities differently, not merely expressions of a personal preference. [15]

Atticus Stonestrom makes a direct proposal about access to publication:

“Traditional journals should ban papers in which AI has played a coauthor-level role, and new venues should be established for the publication of such papers.” [16]

Without a ban, Stonestrom proposes distinguishing such papers and capping their annual publication. He cites authorship and scarce refereeing resources, acknowledges that restrictions may encourage concealment, but argues that this should not determine standards. Even a carefully checked paper could be excluded from a traditional journal. [16]

A young researcher does not need a profession-wide ban to find these positions alarming: a few editors or hiring-committee members can have a decisive effect on a career. Honest disclosure may carry lasting consequences when it can reduce recognition or make a paper ineligible for a journal.

Martin Hairer instead argues that “articles are judged on their merits, independently of the tools being used” and that disclosure should not automatically reduce a paper’s value, while retaining human scrutiny, understanding, and writing as requirements. [17]

What should a postdoc make of these competing messages: use AI responsibly and disclose it, avoid it to demonstrate independent ability, use it or fall behind, yet risk losing recognition by doing so? These are not small differences in taste when employment is at stake.

I have heard colleagues describe the strongest anti-AI views as resistance to an inevitable technology, while others say they reflect a larger, quieter part of the profession. I do not know which claim is correct, since neither a collection of essays nor my conversations establishes what most mathematicians believe.

What is already visible is uncertainty about the consequences of honesty, and that uncertainty deserves an institutional response.

6. What the publication and disclosure data actually show

The data show rapid change without establishing how much AI use is undisclosed or why.

Tammy Kolda and Daniel Appelo count 6,307 primary-mathematics arXiv announcements in August 2026, up 2,785 from 3,522 a year earlier—about 79%, versus 43% across arXiv. [18]

Benoit Henry reports single-author counts of 1,174 and 2,603 for those months (about 122% growth), with 809 later papers mentioning AI. He cautions that the counts are uncertain; single authorship is not evidence of AI use, and an AI mention is not necessarily a carefully classified disclosure. [4]

Xiaoshn Nee, Haobo Zhong, and Xiaomin Ni find growth in 29 of 30 primary mathematics categories; the share of active author units posting at least five papers in January–August rose from 2.45% in 2025 to 3.80% in 2026. [29]

Tara Abrishami’s Epoch AI analysis finds that disclosures of any AI use rose from 3.89% in April 2026 to 25.25% in August (1,453 of 5,754 papers); 337, or 5.86%, disclosed substantial research contributions. The broader category includes writing, computation, and literature review. [19]

Yet three quarters of Epoch’s August papers made no acknowledgment; this group grew from 3,260 in August 2025 to 4,301 in August 2026 (about 32%). Silence does not tell us whether AI was used, and differing corpora and counting conventions prevent simply combining the studies’ totals. [19]

In Kimball Martin’s August 2026 number-theory sample, 12.0% disclosed AI writing while 20.7% were flagged for apparent AI writing. The imperfect detector and unpublished scoring rule make this suggestive only; Martin warns that a score is not a verdict. [20]

These counts neither identify concealed use in individual papers nor prove large-scale concealment, but common sense suggests that incentives to publish faster, coupled with fear of penalties for disclosure, can encourage silence. I suspect some use goes unacknowledged partly because of stigma.

Harlev identifies the underlying incentive: evaluating declared AI work less favorably can punish honest researchers without reliably detecting undisclosed use. [2] We should therefore demand precise disclosures and fair evaluation together, since one without the other creates a predictable conflict.

7. Equal rules require more than equal advice

Access depends not only on whether someone chooses to use AI, but on the models, computing budget, and support available to them. OpenAI’s September account describes an internal model more capable than the public comparator, placing that work in a different setting from a postdoc’s ordinary subscription. [10]

I worry that personal connections to laboratories may become a research advantage. Does staying competitive now require knowing someone who can provide access to an internal system or a large computing budget? What happens to mathematicians who have neither those connections nor an institution able to buy equivalent resources? Such access must be visible in evaluation: a publication list should not conceal the difference between an individual subscription and large, privately supported searches.

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence’s September 29 recommendations warn that proprietary models risk a “two-tier system” and unequal access to public models a “multi-tier hierarchy.” It calls for broad, equitable access. [21]

On 1 October 2026, Claude Max 20x and ChatGPT Pro 200 each cost US$200 monthly; the new ChatGPT Pro 500 costs US$500. Both highest-tier subscriptions total US$700 monthly, or US$8,400 annually, before taxes, exchange charges, and separate computing costs. [30, 31]

Across developing countries and lower-paid academic systems in developed countries, stipends and salaries may leave little for these subscriptions after living expenses, especially when researchers personally fund multiple services. An expense routine for a well-funded department may be unsustainable for an equally capable mathematician elsewhere, rewarding institutional resources and personal finances rather than talent, effort, or the quality of research questions.

Researchers should not have to choose between living expenses and tools increasingly treated as necessary. Institutional support helps, but identical prices do not mean equal access, and subscriptions do not fund thousands of parallel agents.

The Leiden Declaration links AI use to human responsibility, transparency, and its effects on the profession; these principles must apply equally to researchers with and without privileged access. [22]

Orwell’s Animal Farm comes to mind when formal equality coexists with unequal opportunities: I do not want one standard for insiders and another for outsiders, or strict rules for students with exceptions for established names.

8. What future are we offering PhD students?

I welcome the Harvard summit on doctoral education in the age of AI. Its September 17–18 meeting brought together 24 mathematicians, produced recommendations for departmental discussion, and explicitly thanked the graduate students and postdocs who participated in a panel. [23]

Consultation, however, is not the same as an ongoing role in decisions. How will students and postdocs participate in setting the rules that govern their training and evaluation? Who will represent people outside the institutions already most influential in this debate?

The report favors demonstrated mastery over the dissertation alone and says it “need not be a requirement for the thesis to have recorded the first proof.” This may protect students whose work is unexpectedly overtaken, but protection within a PhD program does not automatically carry into the job market. [24]

If an adviser asks a student to wait until an AI-generated argument is fully understood, and someone else posts a less readable version first, will the student still receive comparable recognition? Will thesis and hiring committees use compatible standards?

There can be good educational reasons to restrict tools while students learn a skill; equal treatment need not mean identical training for students and experienced researchers, but the distinction must be explained, bounded, and accompanied by protection against resulting disadvantages.

Senior mathematicians should ask what research opportunities they are preserving for students. If a problem can now be explored quickly using AI, should every such opportunity become another paper on an established researcher’s list, or could some become genuinely collaborative training projects? This concerns mentorship when the supply of attractive projects may change rapidly, not a demand that senior researchers stop research.

Above all, what life are we inviting a talented mathematics graduate to pursue? Many of us entered the subject because we wanted to experience the struggle and joy of discovery: working through failed ideas, finding the right argument, and reaching a moment of understanding through our own effort.

Jonny Evans explains why research produces more than a paper: “The ‘output’ is a person who understands something better,” someone who can carry that understanding into research and teaching. I share his concern that more results do not necessarily mean more capable mathematicians. [33]

Teaching, exposition, and verification are already part of the mathematics I love, but a career centered on checking machine output, teaching calculus, linear algebra, and differential equations to engineering and computer-science students, and explaining results generated inside commercial laboratories may not appeal to people who hoped to become researchers. Calling that concern nostalgia does not answer it.

I fear losing both discovery and professional security while being told that a more demanding system of oral assessments and repeated demonstrations of understanding is the solution. Such assessments may be appropriate, but they do not, by themselves, offer a positive account of the career that follows.

A field that fails to attract and support its next generation cannot preserve itself through inspiring statements alone.

9. What institutions need to say clearly

What I need from the people who hire, promote, edit journals, award grants, and supervise students is not another assurance that mathematics will always matter, but practical answers.

Ben Antieau puts one proposal plainly: “Do not recruit, hire, promote, or praise based on the number of papers.” Daniel Litt argues that sustained mathematical discussion and talks can demonstrate understanding better than papers alone. Henry similarly asks hiring committees to stop counting articles. [25, 26, 4]

These proposals need to become public rules before researchers can rely on them when choosing projects, tools, or publication venues.

I want clear answers in six areas.

Permitted use and responsibility. Which uses of AI are acceptable in research, dissertations, and submitted papers? How do the rules distinguish language editing, coding, literature searches, suggested lemmas, generated proofs, and largely autonomous work? What must every named author understand and be able to defend?

Release and priority. May someone release a proof that is not human-verified? Does a Lean-checked proof have a different status? Is understanding the broad strategy sufficient, or must the details be checked before release? What priority, if any, attaches to an unfinished write-up accompanied by a promise to improve it?

Authorship and attribution. What contributions justify authorship, and what contributions require a different form of recognition? How are the people who supplied prior methods, directed the search, repaired the proof, formalized it, or explained it credited? What must happen when the initial attribution is incomplete?

Hiring, promotion, and publication. Will good, selective mathematics journals accept AI-generated but human-verified proofs under the same standards as other research papers? How much original human input will they require? Will a clear explanation, simplification, or independent reconstruction of an already announced AI result satisfy their standards of originality and significance, or be excluded as exposition? Will those requirements be public before authors invest months in a project?

Will hiring and promotion committees continue to expect the same quantity of publications, journal prestige, citation counts, and h-index as before—or raise those expectations because AI can accelerate production? If understanding and exposition are to count more, what evidence will be accepted in place of those measures, and will it lead to comparable professional opportunities? Will a mathematician working without AI be judged against AI-assisted output rates? Will someone who discloses careful AI use be penalized for doing so? How can candidates challenge decisions based on standards that were never announced?

Training and protection. How will students retain opportunities for independent discovery? How will a student who follows careful verification rules be protected from the resulting delay? How will institutions recognize substantial work that loses chronological priority?

Access and implementation. Who will fund the tools that new expectations require? How will unequal model access and computing budgets be considered? Which rules apply across institutions, when do they begin, and how will students and postdocs participate in reviewing them?

I am asking not for a universal numerical formula for mathematical worth, but for public standards that guide decisions without changing according to a person’s reputation.

10. The future should not be decided over our heads

For the first time, I am seriously considering leaving mathematics—a painful sentence to write after almost twenty-five years of passion, thought, and effort. What makes me consider leaving is not that a machine can do something I cannot, but that I no longer trust the profession to offer a fair and intelligible path forward.

What troubles me most is the possibility that established researchers will keep the advantages of the old system while younger people accept the obligations of a new one. Even when individuals act in good faith, the appearance of that double standard is damaging and should be addressed through transparent rules rather than dismissed as anxiety about technological change.

What I am asking for is a profession in which careful work is not punished for being slow, honesty is not punished for being visible, and access to powerful tools is not confused with mathematical merit.

I would welcome an emergency international meeting, with the reach and seriousness of an ICM, devoted to these questions. It should include doctoral students, postdocs, mathematicians from less wealthy institutions and countries, journal editors, hiring committees, and funding bodies—not only the people who already have the most secure positions. Its aim should be concrete, revisable standards for research, credit, training, and careers, together with a timetable for putting them into practice.

No meeting can settle every question permanently, but we can do better than leaving young researchers to discover the real rules only when an application is rejected.

My deepest fear is not that AI will destroy the career of a mathematician, but that mathematicians will make it unlivable through unequal rules, opaque incentives, and a failure to protect the people who come next.

I do not yet have a settled position on every use of AI in mathematics, but I do have a clear position on fairness: the rules cannot change only for the young.

item.title: Is it fish love?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Mathematicians are humans, and humans have emotions. This essay scratches the surface of an intricate issue behind a very simple question: in what ways and to what extent are mathematicians’ reactions to AI driven by emotion?
item.content:encoded:
Tancredi Schettini Gherardini, postdoctoral researcher based both at the University and at the Max Planck Institute in Bonn.

This reflection starts with a parable I learnt from a recording of Rabbi Dr Abraham Twerski. He came across a young man who was clearly enjoying a fish that he was eating, and asked: ‘Young man, why are you eating that fish?’. And the young man answered ‘because I love fish!’. The Rabbi said: ‘Oh you love the fish, that’s why you took it out of the water and killed it and boiled it? Don’t tell me you love the fish; you love yourself, and because the fish tastes good to you, therefore you took it out of the water and killed it and boiled it.’

The message is that so much of what is usually called love is actually fish-love, i.e. we don’t love the object/person per se but how it/they make us feel. My intuition is that the nature of one’s love for mathematics is intimately related with their views on AI.1

What is it that drives a mathematician to persevere through pain and frustration until a conjecture is proven or disproven? Is it to establish that they are better than others? Is it the satisfaction which comes from reaching a goal that has required so much of their time and energy? Is it the pleasure of knowing the answer to a question they find really interesting? Supposedly, in practice, it will be a mixture of the three. But is there one which overweighs the other two? Is there one which should outweigh the other two?

The answer is deeply personal, and I shall not argue here whether one is better than another. My message is that to understand our own views on AI for mathematics, the most appropriate starting point is an introspective analysis of why we – not as a community, but we-ourselves – love mathematics. This might be a complicated and even disturbing process; but, as Aristotle said, “knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom”.

Let me articulate my argument in a way that is agnostic to the notion of what is a correct motivation for doing mathematics. If mathematicians are most concerned with (possibly interesting) answers to interesting questions, then it is quite hard to argue against the benefits of AI in the subject. One can argue about the negative consequences in the general picture that is wider than mathematics (like environmental damage, privacy issues, monopoly, increase of inequality and unemployment, not to mention the risk of extinction); these are all very serious and well-founded worries which would need many essays, and I shall not deal with them here.2

When restricting to the features that are more specific to our discipline, one can argue about the potential risks in mathematics, which I think mainly boil down to two aspects.

Firstly, losing some important habits and routines essential in the practice of doing good mathematics – mostly those which ensure a deep understanding of the material, such as insightful human interaction, long-term projects and frequent productive struggle, for instance. But, regarding this concern, we have all the tools to deal with it effectively. In fact, we can act upon it by following these good habits ourselves, adapting them in a meaningful way when needed, and transmitting them to the newer generations. To ensure that they keep being part of a mathematician’s workflow, we might require some adjustments on a few fronts, such as the publishing process (where it is desirable to cut out or at least flag AI slop), the hiring process, and many general criteria for judging the quality of a mathematician. This is not just completely in our hands, there is also (almost) complete unanimity: I have never heard any mathematician, optimistic or pessimistic about AI, ever saying that we should give up understanding as a fundamental part of the discipline. To summarise, the temptation of these tools might pull us unwillingly away from understanding, but this risk has already been identified and acknowledged by our community and we have the power to make practical changes discouraging and preventing misuse of AI; in fact a few of these changes have already been implemented and many are currently being discussed.3

The second risk, which I personally consider to be scarier, is that of mathematics losing appeal for young bright minds; once more, it is up to us to not let this happen, illustrating how AI can be embraced in a constructive way, without disrupting the essential features of our field and the understanding-related practices mentioned above. Maybe even more importantly, it is hard to believe that the conservative choice of refusing any use of AI could attract more smart kids to join our community.

As of today, I do not see bigger problems than these two, which are only potential. And so, what are the benefits?

Since a few months ago, most of us have had our own version of Namagiri Thayar. It does not reveal formulas in our dreams, like the Hindu goddess used to do with Ramanujan, but it does so while we are awake and sitting in front of our laptop.4
Our reaction to this fact seems a bit different from the one people had one hundred years ago: I did not find any references of mathematicians from that time complaining about these revelations, nor signing petitions for banning Namagiri Thayar from Ramanujan’s dreams. But now that we all have something equivalent, a different chord was struck in the collective consciousness of our community. A purely emotional one, I argue; because if one’s priority is really the progress of mathematics, then why not embrace this new reality, made of Ramanujan-like moments, driven by AI suggestions, constructions, and results, and Hardy-like moments, trying to make sense of these results, with rigour, clarity and sharp understanding. If one’s love for mathematics is a genuine strive for advancement, and not simply the fish-love of Twerski, then it is impossible to not see the incredible chance we have to push our explorations in this beautiful subject.

The opposite is true if one’s love for mathematics mainly comes from the way that mathematics makes them feel. The feelings of finding a new clever way around a seemingly insurmountable obstruction, constructing a special interesting object that no one had thought of, or proving an important theorem for the first time, are all very much at risk. Because that new argument, example, or proof, could be generated by an LLM operated by someone who may or may not, in many instances, be an expert in the subject; in that case, the emotions which usually come with the mathematical discovery/invention are just gone.

The truth is that inside everyone’s passion for mathematics, and inside everyone’s love for someone or something, there is often a component of genuine and unselfish love, inevitably mixed with some fish-love. We are humans, after all. But if the former prevails, and we are driven by the sincere admiration of the exquisitely intellectual activity that has led humans from a few primitive logical observations to the immense and sophisticated body of knowledge that we have today, we might live the advent of AI with more optimism.

Received 24 September 2026.

  1. Throughout this essay, I will use ‘mathematics’ to mean ‘pure mathematics’ and ‘mathematicians’ to mean ‘pure mathematicians’. Many of the considerations below apply in general, but not all of them. ︎
  2. Let me spend a few words on those global consequences which impact mathematicians as a part of society. The first one is the possible shortage of funding; as of today, theorems in mathematics are a perfectly inelastic good, and there is no good evidence to suggest they should change to be so. Concerning inequality, that is a real issue which should be dealt with; it might be mitigated by the improvement of open-weights models, but there is no guarantee. In any case, this social aspect is somewhat orthogonal to the one I would like to focus on, i.e. the development of mathematics itself. Regarding privacy and intellectual property, they are also real concerns, but it seems possible to deal with them. One can use incognito sessions for sensitive material and do a much more detailed literature search than just quoting the LLM’s output, respectively. ︎
  3. One might argue that a foreseeable future scenario is that in which we delegate all of our thinking to the machines. Once more, that is ultimately up to us, and not a very likely prediction under mildly optimistic assumptions. Finally, if that will really be the case, we will have bigger problems than worrying about mathematics… ︎
  4. With all the obvious caveats, of course, such as hallucinations (although very rare nowadays) and the abundance of AI slop. ︎

item.title: Is There Actually a Good Way to Use AI for Math?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: The post describes a workflow for using AI in theoretical research that I gradually developed while working on these projects. I am especially interested in whether experienced mathematicians use similar methods, even if they do not describe them as prompts or formal workflows.
item.content:encoded:
Yushang Cheng, Undergraduate student, China

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

The author first drafted these reflections in Chinese. AI helped organize them, suggested the mathematical example, and assisted with English translation and rewriting. The author’s full AI use disclosure appears below.

I'm an undergraduate student in China, and much of what I know about research I have had to figure out for myself. I began using AI to explore theoretical questions last year; some of those attempts, including the ones that went wrong, are recorded in my GitHub archive and an SSRN preprint. AI has helped me move forward astonishingly quickly, though I sometimes worry that my mathematical foundations have not kept pace. I still need to put it aside, study on my own, check proofs, and learn to write without it. But I am genuinely curious about certain theoretical questions. Once an idea catches my attention, I want to know where it might lead.

Over time I developed a way of working with AI that feels useful to me. I suspect it could be better, though, so I started asking around. I talked to classmates, posted on forums, and even tried contacting professors and mathematicians. It felt a little like looking for a game walkthrough: surely people who have played much longer than I have must know a few tricks. Most of the AI advice I encountered was about coding, cleaning data, and other routine tasks. Mathematicians seemed a more promising place to look, but their advice was often just as brief: tell AI what you want to prove, ask it to find counterexamples, or have it argue against you. All sensible advice. Still, I had gone looking for a walkthrough and seemed to have come back empty-handed. Perhaps the steps in between are so familiar to experienced researchers that they hardly think to mention them. I thought I might as well share the habits I have developed and ask what you make of them.

Here is a very simple example of the part I find most interesting. Suppose we are studying a continuous function f:[0,1]→ℝf:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} with

f(0)=−1,f(1)=1.f(0)=-1,\qquad f(1)=1.

The intermediate value theorem tells us that there is at least one zero. If we also assume that ff is strictly increasing, the zero is unique. My instinct, however, is to ask whether removing strict monotonicity might make the problem more interesting. Consider

f1(x)=2x−1,f2(x)=323(x−14)(x−12)(x−34).f_1(x)=2x-1, \qquad f_2(x)=\frac{32}{3} \left(x-\frac14\right) \left(x-\frac12\right) \left(x-\frac34\right).

Both functions are continuous and have exactly the same endpoint values, yet the first has one zero and the second has three. Of course, I could put strict monotonicity back, exclude the second function, and return to proving uniqueness. But if I wanted to understand this class of continuous functions in the first place, why should I throw the second one away? I would rather keep it. Now there are two interesting possibilities to study: when is the zero unique, and when can there be several? Can I find conditions that distinguish the cases, and are those conditions necessary? Sometimes I will try to weaken them again. When removing an assumption gives me an interesting counterexample, I want to see whether the counterexample can become part of the theory.

There is another problem I run into if I keep doing this. After enough rounds of removing assumptions, finding counterexamples, and obtaining new results, I may be left with a heap of conditions and conclusions without knowing what each condition is really doing. So I have become rather fond of building the dependencies between results, one step at a time. In the example, we can separate two claims:

continuity + opposite endpoint signs⟹at least one zero,strict increase⟹at most one zero.\begin{aligned} \text{continuity + opposite endpoint signs} &\Longrightarrow \text{at least one zero},\\ \text{strict increase} &\Longrightarrow \text{at most one zero}. \end{aligned}

Together, they give a unique zero. I like this arrangement because I can see what each assumption contributes. If I later find another way to establish “at most one zero,” I do not have to change the existence argument at all.

For a more complicated theory, I might start with a primitive condition AA, derive a meaningful property BB, and then prove something new from BB. I would rather have A⇒B⇒CA\Rightarrow B\Rightarrow C than keep proving everything directly from AA. Sometimes the argument branches: BB leads to CC and DD, and those results together lead to EE. I just find this kind of structure beautiful. At first that was almost the whole reason I liked it. Later I realized that it can do real work. If BB is weaker than AA, the statement B⇒CB\Rightarrow C may apply in settings where AA does not hold; and once BB has been proved somewhere else, I can reuse the same result. The intermediate properties have to mean something, of course. There is no point in making a proof longer just for the sake of a prettier diagram.

This also makes me wonder how far the assumptions in a theorem are from the original problem. If the result depends on a long list of strong technical conditions introduced along the way, I want to know whether they can be derived from more basic objects. In an economics model, for instance, can the conditions be expressed in terms of observed choices, compensated comparisons, or the support of the data? The two functions above offer a small illustration of the information problem. Even if we know the function is continuous and observe both endpoint values exactly, those observations do not tell us whether the zero is unique. The functions look identical to someone who can see only those two values. I often ask AI to construct pairs of models that agree on everything observable but disagree on the property I care about. When such a pair exists, my next question is what extra information would distinguish them, and what, precisely, that information would allow us to conclude.

I came to these habits by taking quite a few wrong turns. My first project concerned a rational-addiction model and what I called an exit mechanism. I was excited by the thought that a rational agent might have a distinct reason to invest in reducing or escaping addictive behavior. But in the model I had written down, the proposed exit or recovery value could be absorbed into the existing state-dependent utility. Behavior therefore could not identify it as a separate mechanism. An idea I had been eager to defend simply did not survive the test. That failure led me somewhere I had not expected: toward questions about what behavior can identify, what sparse compensated comparisons can reveal, and which additional observations really matter. The project eventually led to my SSRN preprint, What Do Finite Compensation Comparisons Reveal? I kept the failed earlier versions on GitHub; they are part of the story, too.

AI has been useful throughout this process. I ask it to remove assumptions, hunt for counterexamples, try proofs, construct observationally equivalent models, and help disentangle which lemmas actually depend on which conditions. I have also seen plenty of arguments that sounded complete until I checked the details. One other habit has grown out of these conversations, and I wonder whether anyone else has noticed the same thing. AI often gives me prose that seems determined to explain everything it has done: “we cannot guarantee uniqueness,” “this assumption is unnecessary,” “the important point is not this but that.” Those sentences can be useful while we are thinking. I just do not much like them in the finished mathematics.

What I like in textbooks is the way a good statement simply tells you the conditions and what follows. For the example above, I would rather write: continuity and opposite endpoint signs give existence; strict increase gives at most one zero; and continuous functions with identical endpoint values can have different numbers of zeros. I can then ask whether the sufficient conditions are also necessary, or how the remaining cases should be characterized. Sometimes replacing a conversational diagnosis with a proper mathematical statement even exposes a gap in my reasoning. The final paper should not have to reproduce every turn of the conversation that brought me there.

One thing about my own method worries me, though. As AI gets better at turning a guess into a mathematical theory, it becomes easier to treat research as a set of buttons to press. I can imagine a seminar where everyone asks the professor for their prompts, but nobody asks how the proof works. I would find that rather sad. The irony is that I’ve already benefited from this method myself, and sometimes I find it hard to stop using it. I know its downsides, but I also want to do this kind of research for a living. I don’t think I’m especially gifted at mathematics, academic jobs are hard to get, publication counts matter, and AI tools keep getting better. It’s very easy for me to tell myself that I have no choice. But that sounds a little like a thief looking at something in a shop window and convincing himself that he has no choice but to steal it. Of course, using AI isn’t stealing. What bothers me is how easily I can make excuses for myself. I can only try to stay aware of this, keep learning the mathematics, and make up my own mind about what AI produces. I shared my prompts because I hope they will help people explore questions they genuinely care about, not just produce more papers. Otherwise, we might end up with more theorems, but less interest in understanding them.

That is roughly how I work at the moment. Perhaps experienced mathematicians have always done something like this and simply never thought of it as a “prompt.” I would love to hear how you use AI to look for counterexamples, how you decide whether a failure is worth studying, and whether you consciously build theories out of reusable intermediate results. I would be just as interested in criticism: what am I missing, and what am I making needlessly complicated? I began this search hoping to find a good walkthrough for myself. It would be nice if sharing our actual experiences helped a few other beginners as well.

Research links. GitHub research archive; SSRN preprint.

AI use disclosure. The research experience, ideas, and initial reflections in this post are my own. I first drafted them in Chinese, in a rather fragmented form. AI helped me organize the original line of thought into a clearer structure, suggested the elementary mathematical example used here, and assisted with the English translation and rewriting. I reviewed the resulting text to ensure that it expresses what I meant and reflects my own experience and uncertainty.

item.title: Paralysis
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “We study mathematics for pretty much the same reasons that we study astronomy. The stars and planets are already out there, and, despite millennia of human observation, there is more we don’t know about them than we do. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Yiannis Sakellaridis, Professor at the Department of Mathematics, Johns Hopkins University. Cross-posted at his blog.

We study mathematics for pretty much the same reasons that we study astronomy. The stars and planets are already out there, and, despite millennia of human observation, there is more we don’t know about them than we do. Same with mathematical truths: they are out there, and have always been; but, as of late, we also have a powerful new telescope, which dramatically changes the scope and volume of exploration. It also affects our perception of geometry: Some stars which used to appear distant are proving much more tractable; others will remain as obscure as before, in need of new ideas for approaching them.

So the story will go, if anyone is left to tell it. Yet, there’s a competing story, according to which “we”, humans, won’t need to understand anything, as this exploration will be completely undertaken by machines. They will get better at everything we do, including finding new conjectures and explaining their discoveries to curious humans, but by the time a person has understood something new, they will be far ahead.

Knowledge is power, and, while I do not know whether such a development is possible, no freedom-loving human should be celebrating the subjugation of human intelligence to artificial intelligence, a Middle Ages in reverse. In more realistic terms, though, it is not about subjugation of humans to machines, but to the owners of those: that’s why so many trillions of investment are flowing into AI. To return the investment, the companies will have to capture staggering percentages of society’s economic output. This requires not just “empowering scientists and mathematicians with tools that accelerate discovery”, but collecting scientific production in-house, being not just a tool but also the owner of intellectual property that will translate itself into patents and pharmaceuticals.

Talking of intellectual property, LLMs which have been trained on my and everyone’s intellectual work, funded by universities and public agencies and published on the arXiv under licenses for non-commercial use, and in journals under various copyright agreements, are now collecting money from my university, which is entering into business agreements in order to remain on the frontier of research. As we enter our prompts into the LLMs, we improve the way in which they will respond to others, without, of course, quoting us. This likely happens whether we have disabled the “training” option or not – or, at least, there is no way to reliably tell, as there is no independent way to audit the inner workings of an AI company.

You would think that a machine powerful enough to outsmart humans would not require such levels of opacity. That it would be able to rush ahead without training data from the last few years of research. That the prompts and any available information on its path to discovery would be made available for the benefit of its future users. That its outputs would be readable and compatible with formalized proofs, and that by solving 400 problems it would generate 1000 conjectures, as humans would have done. Clearly, the machine is not there yet.

But, for the purposes of capturing scientific production, maybe it doesn’t need to get there at all.

Maybe all it takes is vibes taking precedence over expert assessment, and a mathematical community in a state of paralysis. Professional organizations unable to utter a word about the startling misconduct and the theft of intellectual property. Institutions collecting petty donations and staying silent on these same issues. Self-appointed advisory bodies unable to make a determination of whether their advice was followed. A few Fields medalists formulating amateur predictions and repudiating the goals of the medal. And a political environment which was already hostile to science letting the private sector enjoy the gold rush, without any oversight on safety and intellectual property, or any robust plans to create public AI infrastructure for science.

That’s all it will take to convince a generation of aspiring scientists to switch course, and for our society to stop nurturing mathematical skills and understanding. The stultification of humanity will bring the goal of a superhuman machine one step closer.

item.title: Mathematics of the Future
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “Rapid advances in AI are transforming research, and for the growth of mathematical knowledge, this is thrilling. For our profession, however, this raises critical questions: Will there be a role for human mathematicians to play? How should mathematicians be trained and evaluated? […]”
item.content:encoded:
Pavel Etingof (Wikipedia), Professor of Mathematics at MIT, PRIMES Chief Research adviser; and Slava Gerovitch (Wikipedia), Senior Lecturer, Department of Mathematics at MIT, PRIMES Director

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

AI use: ChatGPT was used to improve the exposition of our ideas.

The following is a short summary of a longer text with references, which can be viewed here.

Rapid advances in AI are transforming research, and for the growth of mathematical knowledge, this is thrilling. For our profession, however, this raises critical questions: Will there be a role for human mathematicians to play? How should mathematicians be trained and evaluated? Will there be enough jobs in mathematics? Does it still make sense to pursue a career in mathematics?

We argue that the four main functions of mathematics – discovering truths, being part of human culture and understanding of the world, providing methods for applications, and fostering intellectual growth – will continue to be central in the age of AI. Human mathematicians will still be needed to formulate and prioritize questions, interpret and communicate mathematical results, contribute to AI safety, sustain the social aspects of teaching, and hone analytical and critical thinking skills applicable far beyond academic mathematics.

Given huge uncertainties about the future, nobody can predict which expertise will be in greatest demand. Such expertise cannot be created instantly; it requires years of training, research, and immersion in a professional culture. A strong mathematical community provides a powerful intellectual reserve of such expertise applicable across a wide range of scientific disciplines and industries. This frontier competence can be sustained only by constantly exercising. Just like society needs to maintain fire departments for emergencies, it must support mathematical expertise to preserve and further develop the human capacity to understand and respond to future challenges.

To retain its relevance, however, mathematical culture will need to evolve. For centuries, mathematics relied on the “ownership culture”: competition for priority, with lasting claims to credit for discovering new theorems, enforced through citation and converted into careers, prizes, and reputations via publication lists. This culture is no longer sustainable. If LLMs do most of the heavy lifting, individual credit loses much of its meaning. This may even be healthy: clashing egos have generated much conflict, and mathematics may be better off once egos retreat from “owning” results.

Evaluation criteria based on the ownership culture will have to be revised and rely instead on intellectual agency: broad and deep knowledge, genuine understanding of mathematics and its connections, sound judgment, independent vision, and effective communication skills. Hiring must rely far more on direct mathematical interaction – talks, interviews, sustained conversation – with recommendation letters still important but grounded in substantial personal contact. In the AI era, a theorem proved with heavy AI help should be valued equally to one proved without. Hiring committees should assess mathematicians, not the provenance of their theorems.

The mathematical culture of the future will emphasize a set of new practices. First, it will open a wider mathematical world: instead of focusing on a narrow area, mathematicians will be able to explore a much wider research landscape. Creativity will not disappear; it will simply operate on a frontier moving outward faster than ever. Second, mathematicians will serve as interpreters of massive AI-produced results, helping the wider intellectual community to understand, absorb, connect, and use them. And since the library of available results is always finite while mathematics is infinite, humans will remain contributors, not only readers. Third, mathematicians will use AI to conduct the “big cleanup” of existing mathematical literature, identifying and resolving errors, gaps, obscure arguments, incompatible conventions, and results rediscovered under different names. Mathematicians will use Lean formalization and verification of proofs, but will also complement it with human-readable exposition. The goal is to make the corpus of mathematical literature more reliable and better organized than ever before. Finally, publication formats will evolve to include AI-produced texts, recorded talks, interactive companions, and papers as virtual agents. Publication should become a vibrant infrastructure for navigation, understanding, and further development, rather than a passive record.

Problem solving will decline as professional output but will remain essential as a training tool; discovery-based learning (in the spirit of Alekseev “Abel’s Theorem in Problems and Solutions”) becomes especially valuable. Used well, AI will enable better active and personalized learning: hints rather than solutions, clarifying examples, and diagnostic problems. To test understanding, supervised written tests will need to be supplemented with oral examinations. The aim is to obtain better evidence of subject mastery, not to build a perfect technological defense against dishonesty.

Graduate study will shift emphasis from early specialization and rapid publication toward breadth, depth, communication, and judgment. Faculty-led seminars, reading groups, and advanced courses will grow in importance; as will live mentoring and blackboard exposition. The thesis need not contain the first proof of anything; originality can reside in ideas, methods, questions, connections, or synthesis.

We make a concrete institutional proposal: a small faculty-led lab open to students sharing a background, aiming to combine collaborative research with powerful AI while building the ability to check and understand AI output. The group will meet and brainstorm together, with students taking notes, then the faculty lead will ask AI to respond to the notes, the group will study, check, and discuss the response, with different students focusing on different parts, and the resulting ideas will be written down in a shared document, regularly revised with peer, faculty, and AI comments. The model scales from high-school to graduate research, and success is measured by both the mathematics produced and the growth of the participants.

Finally, we share a few pieces of advice for young mathematicians:

  • Accept fundamental uncertainty: build skills robust across many futures rather than organizing life around AI forecasts.
  • Learn broadly and deeply; follow your heart: resist early specialization, but achieve genuine mastery in some subjects.
  • Put collaboration ahead of competition: find people you enjoy thinking with; help one another understand mathematics.
  • Cultivate intellectual agency, with or without AI: whether using powerful models or building understanding by other means, keep solving problems, asking questions, writing explanations, and testing your knowledge.
  • Plan around strengths and aspirations, not anxiety: keep multiple career paths open, but do not abandon a beloved subject just because some other occupation looks “safe.” Nothing can provide full security in the age of AI; draw on your talents, skills, and knowledge to build your career.

Rather than trying to salvage the old order, we should preserve what is essential – curiosity, knowledge, understanding, intellectual agency, and the joy of doing and sharing mathematics – as we open our minds to the vast and thrilling mathematical world that we can now explore.
